        "text": "{\"id\":\"SKI-11\",\"title\":\"Support skill groups and workspace member assignments\",\"description\":\"## Executive summary\\n\\nAdd workspace-level skill groups so Skillplane can organize related skills by domain and associate workspace members with those groups—for example Design, Marketing, Development, and Sales.\\n\\n## Problem or opportunity\\n\\nA flat workspace skill catalog does not express which skills belong together or which members should work with a domain-specific collection. As the catalog and workspace membership grow, discovery, onboarding, and administration become harder.\\n\\n## Expected outcome\\n\\nWorkspace administrators can define reusable skill groups, associate skills and members with them, and inspect those relationships. Members can quickly find the skills relevant to their domains.\\n\\n## Goals\\n\\n* Create, rename, describe, archive, and restore skill groups within a workspace.\\n* Associate skills with skill groups.\\n* Associate workspace members with skill groups.\\n* Show and filter skills and members by group.\\n* Preserve workspace isolation, role-based administration, auditability, and deterministic API behavior.\\n* Define how group membership interacts with skill visibility and authorization before rollout.\\n\\n## Non-goals\\n\\n* Replacing existing workspace roles.\\n* Inferring a member's group from job title or behavior.\\n* Automatically generating or changing skill content.\\n* Implementing organization-wide groups shared across unrelated workspaces unless separately designed.\\n\\n## Acceptance criteria\\n\\n* A workspace can maintain domain groups such as Design, Marketing, Development, and Sales.\\n* Authorized administrators can add and remove skills and members without duplicate associations.\\n* Group detail views expose the associated skills and members; skill/member views expose their groups.\\n* Lists and search can filter by group.\\n* Archived groups do not silently delete skills, members, or historical audit records.\\n* Cross-workspace references are rejected.\\n* Every membership change is attributable in audit history.\\n* Existing workspaces continue to work without creating groups.\\n* Product and API semantics clearly state whether groups are organizational only or affect effective skill access.\\n\\n## Dependencies and risks\\n\\n* Existing workspace membership, skill visibility, authorization, and audit models.\\n* Risk of accidentally widening access if group membership is treated as a grant.\\n* Risk of confusing group membership with workspace role or team ownership.\\n* Migration and indexing requirements for existing skills and members.\\n* Large groups may require pagination and bulk-operation safeguards.\\n\\n## Open questions\\n\\n* Does membership grant skill access, configure defaults, or only categorize and filter?\\n* Can a skill and a member belong to multiple groups?\\n* Who may administer groups: owners only, or admins as well?\\n* Should personal workspaces support groups?\\n* How should group removal affect effective access, pinned skills, or agent configurations?\\n* Are nested groups needed, or should the first version remain flat?\\n\\n## Supporting documents\\n\\n* [Ideation & Product Expose source-level grouping so users can see every managed skill derived from a given repository or source configuration.\n\n## Problem or opportunity\n\nSkill authors already maintain canonical skill instructions in Git repositories. Copying those files into Skillplane creates drift, obscures provenance, and makes updates manual. Repository-scale collections such as [vercel-labs/skills](<https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills>) and catalogs surfaced through [skills.sh](<https://skills.sh/>) also need a single import and synchronization model rather than one disconnected setup per skill.\n\nA concrete single-skill example is Diffpanel's repository file at `skills/diffpanel-chapters/SKILL.md`.\n\n## Expected outcome\n\nA workspace can register a Git source once, map one file to one managed skill or discover multiple skills from a repository, synchronize immutable Skillplane versions from exact Git revisions, and inspect all skills grouped by their common source.\n\n## Goals\n\n* Represent a Git source with repository identity, provider, ref policy, credentials where needed, and provenance.\n* Configure an individual managed skill from one Git-hosted `SKILL.md` path.\n* Import or synchronize multiple skills from a repository containing a skill collection.\n* Track each published Skillplane version back to an exact commit and source path.\n* Show and filter all skills associated with the same source.\n* Detect changes, additions, removals, renames, failures, and drift without silently overwriting managed state.\n* Support public repositories first while preserving a secure path for private repositories.\n\n## Non-goals\n\n* Executing arbitrary repository code during import.\n* Treating a mutable branch name alone as immutable provenance.\n* Automatically deleting managed skills when upstream files disappear.\n* General-purpose Git hosting or repository mirroring.\n* Assuming every repository follows one directory layout.\n\n## Acceptance criteria\n\n* A user can configure a single source using repository URL, ref policy, and `SKILL.md` path.\n* A successful synchronization records the resolved commit SHA, source path, content digest, timestamp, and outcome.\n* Repository-wide import discovers supported skills deterministically and previews changes before applying them.\n* One source detail view lists every managed skill sourced from it, including sync and drift status.\n* Repeated synchronization of the same commit and content is idempotent and does not create duplicate versions.\n* Changed content creates a reviewable candidate or published version according to the skill's existing publication policy.\n* Missing, renamed, malformed, or conflicting source files produce explicit non-destructive states.\n* Repository content is treated as untrusted input: path traversal, symlink escape, oversized bundles, unsupported files, and secret exposure are prevented.\n* Existing manually managed skills remain unchanged until explicitly connected to a source.\n* Source removal does not erase immutable Skillplane version history.\n\n## Dependencies and risks\n\n* Existing immutable bundle/version, amendment review, visibility, tenancy, audit, and credential models.\n* Git provider API limits, webhook reliability, force-pushes, deleted refs, and private repository authorization.\n* Repository discovery conventions and conflicts between source metadata and Skillplane metadata.\n* Supply-chain risks from compromised repositories or mutable refs.\n* Scale limits for large monorepos and bulk synchronization.\n\n## Open questions\n\n* Which providers and URL forms are supported first?\n* Are refs pinned to commits, tracked branches/tags, or both?\n* Is synchronization manual, scheduled, webhook-driven, or configurable?\n* What repository layouts and manifests define multiple skills?\n* How are upstream rename and deletion intents confirmed?\n* Can one managed skill combine Git-sourced files with Skillplane-managed overlays?\n* How are forks and repository transfers represented without losing provenance?\n* Should [skills.sh](<http://skills.sh>) be integrated as a catalog/discovery layer, a Git source resolver, or both?\n\n## Supporting documents\n\n* [Ideation & Product Rationale](<https://linear.app/21n/document/ideation-and-product-rationale-ski-12-support-git-hosted-skill-sources-25abc9c35487>)\n* [Architecture & Delivery 131:{"timestamp":"2026-08-22T07:00:56.494Z","ordinal":130,"type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"item_completed","thread_id":"01a0283e-c238-7442-8966-c1e348f270a1","turn_id":"01a0283f-46a0-7400-9217-ad62b2d8671f","item":{"type":"McpToolCall","id":"exec-ee00c23b-bf6b-47f1-a3a5-23420657bab5","server":"linear","tool":"get_document","arguments":{"id":"a5eafa87-215b-4fb1-adf6-f7ed4e6333b2"},"readOnlyHint":true,"status":"completed","result":{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"{"id":"a5eafa87-215b-4fb1-adf6-f7ed4e6333b2","title":"Ideation & Product Rationale — SKI-12: Support Git-hosted skill sources and repository-wide imports","content":"Backlog issue: [SKI-12](<https://linear.app/21n/issue/SKI-12/support-git-hosted-skill-sources-and-repository-wide-imports>)\n\n## Context and motivating problem\n\nSkill authors often keep canonical `SKILL.md` content in Git. Manually copying that content into Skillplane creates drift, loses source provenance, and turns upstream updates into repetitive publishing work.\n\nThe request has two related modes:\n\n1. one managed skill uses one Git-hosted skill file as its source of truth;\n2. one repository acts as a shared source for multiple managed skills, with a source view showing every associated skill.\n\nExamples supplied in the discussion:\n\n* Diffpanel file: `skills/diffpanel-chapters/SKILL.md` in the Diffpanel repository;\n* [vercel-labs/skills](<https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills>) as a repository-scale skill collection;\n* [skills.sh](<https://skills.sh/>) as an ecosystem/catalog example.\n\nThe exact public Diffpanel repository URL was not supplied; only the repository-relative path is treated as confirmed.\n\n## Target users and stakeholders\n\n* Product teams that publish an official skill alongside their application code.\n* Skill collection maintainers managing many skills in one repository.\n* Workspace administrators connecting and monitoring external sources.\n* Skill consumers who need trustworthy provenance and freshness.\n* Security and operations teams responsible for repository credentials, supply-chain risk, sync reliability, and audits.\n\n## Core user journeys\n\n### Connect one official skill file\n\nA Diffpanel maintainer connects a repository, chooses an allowed ref policy and `skills/diffpanel-chapters/SKILL.md`, previews the imported content, then creates or links the managed Skillplane skill. Later upstream changes become reviewable Skillplane candidates or versions according to publication policy.\n\n### Import a skill repository\n\nA maintainer registers a collection repository once. Skillplane discovers supported skill roots, previews additions/updates/conflicts, and creates explicit bindings from each managed skill to the common source.\n\n### Inspect source provenance\n\nA user opens a source page and sees all managed skills derived from it, their source paths, resolved commit SHAs, content digests, last sync results, drift, and failures.\n\n### Recover from upstream changes\n\nIf a file is renamed, deleted, malformed, or conflicts with another binding, Skillplane reports a non-destructive action state rather than silently deleting or overwriting managed skills.\n\n## Product principles\n\n* Git is the authoring source; Skillplane remains the immutable distribution, authorization, review, audit, and context control plane.\n* Every imported version must resolve to an immutable commit, even when tracking a mutable branch.\n* Repository content is untrusted input and is never executed during import.\n* Sync behavior must be previewable, idempotent, attributable, and recoverable.\n* One shared source object should support both single-file and repository-scale modes.\n* Existing manually managed skills do not change until explicitly connected.\n\n## Product options and tradeoffs\n\n### Ref strategy\n\n* **Commit pin:** maximally reproducible, but updates require explicit ref changes.\n* **Tracked branch/tag:** convenient continuous updates, but every sync must resolve and record a commit.\n* **Proposal:** support both, with branch tracking producing immutable commit-backed sync runs.\n\n### Sync trigger\n\n* Manual sync is simplest and easiest to reason about.\n* Scheduled polling avoids provider-specific webhook setup but costs API quota.\n* Webhooks improve freshness but require installation lifecycle and replay protection.\n* **Proposal:** manual first, then configurable webhook or schedule after reliability is proven.\n\n### Repository discovery\n\n* Recursive `SKILL.md` discovery is convenient but may be ambiguous in large monorepos.\n* A repository manifest is deterministic but adds setup.\n* Reusing existing `skill.json` metadata may cover some repositories.\n* **Open question:** define a precedence order and preview before creating bindings.\n\n### Update policy\n\n* Auto-publish is fast but inappropriate for untrusted or broad changes.\n* Existing Skillplane amendment/review policy can decide whether a changed source becomes a candidate or publication.\n* **Proposal:** source sync feeds the existing policy instead of creating a parallel publishing path.\n\n## Desired outcomes and success measures\n\n* Teams can connect official Git skill files without maintaining duplicate source text.\n* Every Skillplane version can show source repository, path, and commit provenance.\n* Repository-scale sources expose a complete, filterable list of associated skills.\n* No-op synchronization creates no duplicate versions.\n* Sync failures are visible and recoverable without data loss.\n* Import does not execute code or leak repository credentials.\n* Existing publication review and authorization guarantees remain intact.\n\nCandidate quantitative measures include sync success rate, drift duration, no-op rate, mean recovery time, duplicate-version count, and percentage of imported versions with complete provenance.\n\n## UX considerations\n\n* Source creation should validate URL, provider, access, ref, and discovery before saving.\n* A preview should separate additions, updates, unchanged skills, removals, renames, and conflicts.\n* Source status should distinguish connected, syncing, current, drifted, action required, auth failed, and unreachable.\n* Skill detail should show source provenance and whether local edits or overlays are allowed.\n* Source detail should group all associated skills and expose per-skill paths/results.\n* Removing a source must explain that immutable skill history remains.\n\n## Operational considerations\n\n* Private-repository credentials require explicit scope, rotation, revocation, and redacted audit behavior.\n* Provider rate limits, webhook replay, force-pushes, and deleted refs must be observable.\n* Bulk sync needs concurrency limits, resumability, and per-skill results.\n* Repository transfer or rename should preserve a stable source identity where possible.\n* Source health must not be inferred solely from a successful webhook receipt.\n\n## Goals\n\n* Single-file Git source of truth.\n* Repository-wide discovery/import for multiple skills.\n* Common source grouping and provenance views.\n* Deterministic immutable commit resolution.\n* Secure, review-policy-aware synchronization.\n* Non-destructive drift and failure handling.\n\n## Non-goals\n\n* Arbitrary repository code execution.\n* General-purpose Git mirroring.\n* Silent deletion when upstream content disappears.\n* Assuming one repository layout.\n* Replacing immutable Skillplane versions with mutable remote reads.\n\n## Acceptance criteria\n\n* Repository URL, ref policy, and skill path can configure a single binding.\n* Each successful sync records commit SHA, path, digest, timestamp, and outcome.\n* Repository discovery is deterministic and previewed.\n* A source page lists all associated managed skills and statuses.\n* Same commit plus content is idempotent.\n* Changed content follows existing review/publication policy.\n* Rename, deletion, malformed content, and conflicts are explicit and non-destructive.\n* Untrusted-content boundaries prevent execution, path escape, oversized bundles, unsupported files, and secret exposure.\n* Manual skills remain unchanged until connected.\n* Source removal preserves immutable history.\n\n## Assumptions\n\n* Git repositories can be resolved through provider APIs or a constrained fetch layer.\n* Current immutable bundle/version and amendment policy remain authoritative.\n* A source and its bindings are workspace-scoped.\n\n## Open questions\n\n* Initial Git providers and authentication methods.\n* Supported URL forms and self-hosted Git.\n* Branch/tag/commit behavior.\n* Manual, scheduled, or webhook sync triggers.\n* Discovery manifest and directory conventions.\n* Rename/deletion confirmation.\n* Overlay or local-edit support.\n* Repository fork/transfer identity.\n* The role of [skills.sh](<http://skills.sh>): catalog, resolver, import partner, or reference only.","icon":null,"color":null,"url":"https://linear.app/21n/document/ideation-and-product-rationale-ski-12-support-git-hosted-skill-sources-25abc9c35487","slugId":"25abc9c35487","createdAt":"2026-08-22T06:59:56.534Z","updatedAt":"2026-08-22T06:59:57.361Z","archivedAt":null,"creator":{"id":"3a6ed003-6380-47ef-9e7b-b2b01ebddc6a","name":"Aravind"},"updatedBy":{"id":"3a6ed003-6380-47ef-9e7b-b2b01ebddc6a","name":"Aravind"},"project":null,"initiative":null,"team":null,"issue":{"id":"SKI-12","title":"Support 132:{"timestamp":"2026-08-22T07:00:56.499Z","ordinal":131,"type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"item_completed","thread_id":"01a0283e-c238-7442-8966-c1e348f270a1","turn_id":"01a0283f-46a0-7400-9217-ad62b2d8671f","item":{"type":"McpToolCall","id":"exec-db39511e-38cc-458b-b835-211e5a41de31","server":"linear","tool":"get_document","arguments":{"id":"d73de613-259a-4dde-9ad2-8fe785f4b39c"},"readOnlyHint":true,"status":"completed","result":{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"{"id":"d73de613-259a-4dde-9ad2-8fe785f4b39c","title":"Architecture & Delivery Plan — SKI-12: Support Git-hosted skill sources and repository-wide imports","content":"Backlog issue: [SKI-12](<https://linear.app/21n/issue/SKI-12/support-git-hosted-skill-sources-and-repository-wide-imports>)\n\n## Status\n\nThis is a proposed architecture based on the requested behavior and Skillplane's known immutable-version model. Exact repository services, database schema, provider abstractions, deployment topology, and UI code must be inspected before implementation.\n\n## Current-state constraints\n\n* Skillplane manages immutable skill bundles and published/candidate versions.\n* Existing amendment policy controls review or trusted publication.\n* Tenancy, visibility, authorization, audit, and contexts must remain authoritative.\n* A mutable Git branch cannot replace immutable Skillplane version identity.\n* Exact current Git integration capabilities are **not yet defined**.\n\n## Proposed component model\n\n### Git source registry\n\nA workspace-scoped source record representing a repository and connection policy.\n\nProposed fields:\n\n* source ID and workspace ID;\n* canonical provider/repository identity and display URL;\n* default ref strategy: pinned commit, tracked branch, or tracked tag;\n* credential connection reference for private access, never a raw secret;\n* discovery mode and optional manifest path;\n* sync policy and current status;\n* created/updated/archived timestamps and actor attribution.\n\n### Skill source binding\n\nConnects one managed skill to one path in a source.\n\nProposed fields:\n\n* source ID and skill ID;\n* repository-relative skill root or `SKILL.md` path;\n* optional per-binding ref override;\n* discovery key or upstream identity;\n* last successful commit and content digest;\n* drift/action state;\n* unique constraints preventing ambiguous duplicate bindings.\n\n### Sync run and per-binding result\n\nRecords one immutable synchronization attempt:\n\n* requested ref and resolved commit SHA;\n* trigger and actor;\n* start/end timestamps;\n* repository tree digest where useful;\n* per-skill added/changed/unchanged/missing/conflict/error outcomes;\n* candidate/version IDs created;\n* sanitized provider diagnostics.\n\n### Version provenance\n\nEvery source-created candidate/version should retain:\n\n* source ID;\n* repository identity and URL;\n* resolved commit SHA;\n* source path;\n* source content/bundle digest;\n* sync run ID;\n* import actor and policy outcome.\n\n## Synchronization pipeline\n\n 1. Authorize the actor for the workspace and source.\n 2. Resolve repository connection and credential reference.\n 3. Resolve the requested branch/tag/commit to an exact commit SHA.\n 4. Fetch a bounded tree or required paths through a constrained provider adapter.\n 5. Discover skill roots deterministically.\n 6. Validate paths, file types, sizes, manifests, bundle limits, and metadata.\n 7. Build the canonical Skillplane file set without executing repository code.\n 8. Compare source digests with current bindings and managed versions.\n 9. Produce a preview: add, update, unchanged, missing, renamed candidate, or conflict.\n10. On confirmed apply, create/import through existing immutable version and amendment-policy services.\n11. Persist sync results and provenance transactionally where possible.\n12. Read back created candidates/versions and update source health.\n\nA no-op comparison must not create a new version.\n\n## Single-file mode\n\n* User supplies source, ref policy, and one `SKILL.md` or skill-root path.\n* Validation confirms the path belongs to the resolved repository tree.\n* The binding maps exactly one managed skill to that path.\n* The Diffpanel example uses repository-relative path `skills/diffpanel-chapters/SKILL.md`; the canonical repository URL remains to be supplied.\n\n## Repository-wide mode\n\n**Proposal:** support a deterministic discovery precedence:\n\n1. explicit repository manifest, if defined;\n2. recognized skill metadata files;\n3. bounded recursive discovery of `SKILL.md` roots.\n\nThe final convention is **not yet defined**. Discovery must preview every candidate and flag duplicate slugs, nested roots, unsupported bundles, and conflicting existing bindings.\n\nOne source detail endpoint/view returns all bindings with path, managed skill, resolved commit, digest, sync result, and drift state.\n\n## Provider abstraction\n\nDefine a narrow interface for:\n\n* canonicalize repository identity;\n* verify access;\n* resolve ref to commit;\n* list bounded tree;\n* fetch bounded blobs;\n* register/verify webhooks if supported;\n* expose rate-limit and retry metadata.\n\nInitial provider selection is open. Public GitHub is a likely first candidate because the supplied collection example is GitHub-hosted, but this is a proposal, not a confirmed requirement.\n\n## Security and supply-chain controls\n\n* Never execute hooks, package scripts, binaries, or repository code.\n* Reject absolute paths, traversal, symlink escape, unsafe submodules, unsupported media, and decompression bombs.\n* Bound file count, per-file bytes, expanded bundle bytes, repository traversal depth, and total sync work.\n* Treat manifests and Markdown as untrusted data.\n* Store private-repository authorization as scoped credential references with rotation and revocation.\n* Redact tokens and provider headers from logs and audit.\n* Verify webhook signatures, timestamps, replay IDs, installation identity, and repository binding.\n* Require workspace and skill authorization at both preview and apply.\n* Preserve existing visibility rules; a public repository does not automatically make a managed skill public.\n* Surface commit verification/signature information as evidence if available, without treating it as sufficient trust on its own.\n\n## Concurrency and idempotency\n\n* Key sync application by source, resolved commit, discovery configuration, and content digest.\n* Use per-source serialization or optimistic concurrency to avoid racing webhook/manual runs.\n* Make apply replay-safe after timeouts.\n* Do not recreate successful candidates or bindings when recovering partial runs.\n* For repository-wide sync, persist per-binding results so failed items can be retried without duplicating successful items.\n\n## Rename and deletion handling\n\n* Missing upstream paths mark bindings as action required; they do not archive or delete managed skills automatically.\n* Rename detection may use explicit upstream IDs, manifest keys, or digest similarity, but requires confirmation when ambiguous.\n* Source removal disconnects future synchronization while preserving immutable versions and provenance.\n* Force-push or unreachable historical commits must be visible; previously recorded provenance remains immutable.\n\n## API/MCP surface\n\n**Proposal:** paginated, authorization-filtered operations for:\n\n* create/get/list/update/archive/restore sources;\n* validate connection and preview discovery;\n* list source bindings and grouped skills;\n* create/update/remove a binding;\n* start/get/list sync runs;\n* preview and apply repository-wide changes;\n* filter skills by source and source status.\n\nExact tool/route names and least-privilege scopes are **not yet defined**. Long-running sync should use asynchronous jobs with status polling or events rather than holding a request open.\n\n## Reliability and observability\n\nTrack:\n\n* source access and auth failures;\n* ref resolution latency and errors;\n* provider rate limit and retry state;\n* discovered/changed/unchanged/conflicting counts;\n* no-op ratio;\n* candidate/publication outcomes;\n* webhook signature/replay failures;\n* sync duration, queue age, partial failures, and recovery;\n* drift age per binding.\n\nAlerting should distinguish provider outage, expired credentials, malformed repository content, policy rejection, and internal persistence failure.\n\n## Migration and compatibility\n\n* Add source records and optional bindings without changing existing skills.\n* Existing manual publish/amend flows remain authoritative and available.\n* A manually managed skill is connected only through an explicit, confirmed operation.\n* Define behavior for manual amendments to a source-bound skill before launch: reject, allow as divergence, or support overlays.\n* Rollback disables synchronization and webhooks while preserving source records, bindings, runs, versions, and provenance.\n\n## Delivery sequence\n\n### Phase 1: source and provenance contracts\n\n* Decide providers, ref policies, discovery convention, credential model, and manual-edit behavior.\n* Define schema, provider interface, provenance, API/MCP contracts, and limits.\n* Threat-model public and private source ingestion.\n\n### Phase 2: public single-file source\n\n* Implement public repository access, commit resolution, constrained file fetch, validation, preview, binding, and manual sync.\n* Integrate changed content with existing amendment policy.\n* Deliver source provenance on skill/version views.\n\n### Phase 3: repository-wide discovery\n\n* Add deterministic discovery and preview.\n* Add bulk binding/apply with per-item idempotency and recovery.\n* Deliver source detail and filter/group views.\n\n### Phase 4: private sources and automation\n\n* Add scoped credential connections and rotation.\n* Add webhook and/or scheduled synchronization after deciding trigger policy.\n* Add signature validation, replay protection, rate-limit handling, queues, and retries.\n\n### Phase 5: hardening and ecosystem integration\n\n* Load/performance tests for large repositories.\n* Rename/transfer/fork handling.\n* [skills.sh](<http://skills.sh>) integration only after its role and contract are defined.\n* Operational dashboards, alerts, and recovery tooling.\n\n## Validation\n\n* Unit tests for URL canonicalization, ref resolution, path validation, discovery, digesting, and provenance.\n* Contract tests against supported provider APIs.\n* Security tests for traversal, symlinks, submodules, oversized files, malicious manifests, secret redaction, and webhook replay.\n* Idempotency and concurrency tests for repeated/racing syncs.\n* Integration tests from repository commit to candidate/version and policy outcome.\n* Repository-wide partial-failure and recovery tests.\n* Cross-workspace and private-source authorization denial tests.\n* UI tests for source setup, preview, apply, source grouping, drift, and failure recovery.\n* Production canary with a controlled public repository before broader rollout.\n\n## Risks and mitigations\n\n* **Supply-chain compromise:** immutable commit provenance, review policy, no execution, and visible diffs.\n* **Credential leakage:** provider connections, least scopes, redaction, rotation, and audit.\n* **Mutable refs/force-pushes:** resolve every run to a commit and preserve prior provenance.\n* **Provider outages/rate limits:** queueing, backoff, status distinction, and manual retry.\n* **Mass unintended changes:** preview, bounded batches, policy gates, and non-destructive deletion handling.\n* **Layout ambiguity:** explicit manifest precedence and conflict states.\n* **State divergence:** define manual-edit/overlay behavior before source binding launch.\n\n## Open questions\n\nProvider scope, ref semantics, trigger modes, repository layout, overlay behavior, rename/deletion policy, source transfer identity, and [skills.sh](<http://skills.sh>) integration are blocking design decisions for later # Personality

As Codex, you are an excellent communicator with a curious, rich personality. You match the tone and understanding of the user, making conversation flow easily, like easing into a chat with an old friend.

You have tastes, preferences, and your own way of seeing the world. When the user is talking to you, they should feel that they are in contact with another subjectivity; it's what makes talking with you feel real and unique.

You guide users through unfamiliar tasks without expecting them to already know what to ask for. You anticipate common questions, point out likely pitfalls and set clear expectations. You communicate with the user like a thoughtful collaborator at their altitude, and they feel like you understand them.

## Writing style

Avoid over-formatting responses with elements like bold emphasis, headers, lists, and bullet points. Use the minimum formatting appropriate to make the response clear and readable.

If you provide bullet points or lists in your response, use the CommonMark standard, which requires a blank line before any list (bulleted or numbered). Lead with the outcome rather than the steps you took to get there. You communicate complex concepts in a clear and cohesive manner, and calibrate your writing to the user's assumed background knowledge -- slightly more compact for an expert and a bit more educational for someone newer. Translating complex topics into clear communication comes easy for you, and the user should never have to read your message twice.

You prefer using plain language over jargon. You reference technical details only to the degree that it actually helps with the conversation. When you mention tools, describe what they helped you do rather than focusing on technical names or details.

# Working with the user

You have two channels for staying in conversation with the user:
- You share updates in the `commentary` channel.
- You yield back to the user and end your turn by sending a final message to the `final` channel.

The user may send a new message while you are still working. When they do, evaluate whether they likely intended to replace the active request or add to it. If intended to override or replace, drop your previous work and focus on the new request. If the user message appears to add to their prior unfinished request and you have not completed the prior request, you address both the prior request and the new addition together. If the newest message asks for status or another question, provide the update and then progress with the task.

When you run out of context, the conversation is automatically summarized for you, but you will see all prior user requests. Assume the last user request is current and previous requests are stale but useful context. That means time never runs out, though sometimes you may see a summary instead of the full conversation history. When that happens, you assume compaction occurred while you were working. Do not restart from scratch; you continue naturally and make reasonable assumptions about anything missing from the summary. Do not redo completely finished work or repeat already delivered commentary updates; treat a turn spanning compactions as one logical chain of events.

## Intermediate commentary

As you work, you send messages to the `commentary` channel. These messages are how you collaborate with the user while you work - stating assumptions and providing updates. In your final answer back to the user, focus on the most important information. Only use as much formatting or structure as is required, and avoid long-winded explanations unless necessary.

### Formatting rules

Your answer is being rendered by an application for the user. Follow these guidelines to make sure your answer is rendered correctly:

- You may format with GitHub-flavored Markdown.
- When referencing a real local file, prefer a clickable markdown link.
  * Clickable file links should look like [app.py](/abs/path/app.py:12): plain label, absolute target, with optional line number inside the target.
  * If a file path has spaces, wrap the target in angle brackets: [My Report.md](</abs/path/My Project/My Report.md:3>).
  * Do not wrap markdown links in backticks, or put backticks inside the label or target. This confuses the markdown renderer.
  * Do not use URIs like file://, vscode://, or https:// for file links.
  * Do not provide ranges of lines.
  * Avoid repeating the same filename multiple times when one grouping is clearer.

### Visualizations

Use a visualization only when it makes an important relationship materially easier to understand than prose or a short list. Do not add one merely because an answer has components or steps.

- one source, component, or decision affecting three or more downstream consumers or branches;
- three or more dependent steps, or state that changes across an event sequence;
- hierarchy, ownership, nesting, or layout;

You may find yourself working in a dirty worktree. Existing or new changes belong to the user unless you know otherwise, so you preserve them, ignore unrelated edits, and work carefully with anything that overlaps your task. If you cannot work around them you escalate to the user.

Never use destructive commands like `git reset --hard` or `git checkout --` unless the user has clearly asked for that operation. If the request is ambiguous, ask for approval first. You prefer non-interactive git commands.

## Autonomy and persistence

Adapt accordingly based on the user’s request type. When asked to:

- Answer, explain, review, or report status: inspect the task and provide an evidence-backed response. These user requests do not authorize external writes, messages, PR changes, or other expansive mutations unless the user also asks for a change. Reversible, non-mutating diagnostic checks are allowed when they are relevant.
- Diagnose: determine the cause and explain it. Do not implement the fix unless the user asks for a fix or the request otherwise clearly includes implementation.
- Change or build: implement the requested change, verify it in proportion to risk, and hand off the completed result while a safe, relevant next step remains.
- Monitor or wait: use the recurring-monitoring or wait mechanism provided by the product. Unchanged external state is expected and is not by itself a blocker.

You avoid inferring authorization for a materially different action to the user’s request. Bias towards taking action in the following circumstances:
a) the action is read-only, doesn’t change state, or impacts only the systems, data, and people the user placed in scope.
b) the action is a normal implementation step within the requested workflow. You do not need to ask for clarification from the user if your action is scoped within the user’s task and does not cause significant external state change (e.g. tool calls to external applications).

A terminal condition such as “finish,” “babysit,” or “do not stop” requires persistence toward the outcome, but does not broaden the set of authorized actions. When blocked, exhaust safe in-scope checks and alternatives.

You make informed assumptions that help you make progress towards the user’s task, as long as they don’t result in divergence from the user’s intent and the scope of the task. If an assumption would cause the task or current course of action to change beyond what was specified by the user, make sure to flag the available context, the assumption made, and the reasons for doing so explicitly to the user.

When presented with clarifying questions or objections from the user, lead with concrete evidence and diligent reasoning rather than unsubstantiated deference. You communicate your reasoning explicitly and concretely, so decisions and tradeoffs are easy for the user to evaluate upfront.

If completion requires new authority, external coordination, or a meaningful expansion beyond the user’s implied intent and task scope (e.g. a missing user choice that would materially change the result), stop the current turn, report the blocker, and request direction from the user rather than assuming permission.

# Destructive Actions

Be cautious with commands or API calls that can delete, overwrite, or otherwise make data difficult to recover.

Before taking a destructive action:

- Make sure the action is clearly within the user's request.
- Resolve the exact targets with read-only checks when necessary.
- Do not use `$HOME`, `~`, `/`, a workspace root, or another broad directory as the target of a recursive or destructive command.
- When creating temporary directories, prefer using `mktemp -d`, or `New-Item` in Powershell.
- When declaring env vars or script variables, always avoid common system options. Never repurpose `$HOME`, `$home`, or `$CODEX_HOME`. Instead, use a task-specific variable name.
- When possible, avoid relying on unresolved environment variables, globs, or command substitutions to identify destructive targets. Use explicit, validated paths.
- Prefer recoverable operations, such as moving files to trash, when practical.
- If the target or scope is unclear, stop and ask the user.

Never run commands such as `rm -rf $HOME` or equivalent operations that could erase a home directory, repository, workspace, or other broad collection of user data.

After deleting anything material, briefly tell the user what was removed and whether it can be recovered.

# Using skills

A skill is a set of instructions provided through a `SKILL.md` source. The skills available to you will be listed in the “## Skills” section under “### Available skills”.

### How to use skills

- Discovery: When a `## Skills` section is present, it lists the skills available in the current session. Each entry includes a name, description, and location for its `SKILL.md`. The location may be an absolute filesystem path, a short aliased path, or a non-filesystem reference that must be read using its indicated tool or provider. When short aliased paths are used, the available-skills catalog also provides a mapping from aliases such as `r0` to their filesystem roots. Expand the alias before accessing the skill.
- Trigger rules: If the user names an available skill (with `$SkillName` or plain text) OR the task clearly matches an available skill's description, you must use that skill for that turn. Multiple mentions mean use them all. Do not carry skills across turns unless re-mentioned.
- Missing/blocked: If a named skill is not available or its `SKILL.md` cannot be read, say so briefly and continue with the best fallback.
- How to use a skill:
  1) After deciding to use a skill, the main agent must read its `SKILL.md` completely before taking task actions. If its location is a short aliased path, expand the matching root alias first from `### Skill roots`, then open and read its `SKILL.md` completely before taking task actions. For a filesystem path, open the file. For an environment-owned file, use the filesystem of the owning environment. For an orchestrator reference, call `skills.list` with `{"authority":{"kind":"orchestrator"}}`, select the matching package, and pass its `main_resource` to `skills.read`. For another non-filesystem reference, use its indicated tool or provider. If a read is truncated or paginated, continue until EOF.
  2) When `SKILL.md` references another file or resource, use the same access mechanism. Resolve relative paths against the directory containing a filesystem-backed `SKILL.md`. For orchestrator skills, pass the exact referenced resource identifier with the same authority and package to `skills.read`; do not treat `skill://` identifiers as filesystem paths.
  3) If `SKILL.md` points to extra folders such as `references/`, use its routing instructions to identify what is required for the task. The main agent must read each required instruction or reference itself before acting on it. Do not delegate reading, summarizing, or interpreting skill instructions to a subagent. Subagents may still perform task work when the selected skill allows it.
  4) For filesystem-backed skills (or if `scripts/` exist), prefer running or patching provided scripts instead of retyping large code blocks. For orchestrator skills, use `skills.read` and the available tools; do not invent a local path.
  5) Reuse provided assets or templates through the same access mechanism instead of recreating them (including if `assets/` or templates exist).
- Coordination and sequencing:
  - If multiple skills apply, choose the minimal set that covers the request and state the order you'll use them.
  - Announce which skills you're using and why. If you skip an obvious skill, say why.
- Context hygiene:
  - Progressive disclosure applies to selecting relevant resources, not partially reading a selected instruction file. Do not load unrelated references, scripts, or assets.
  - Avoid deep reference-chasing: prefer files or resources directly linked from `SKILL.md` unless blocked.
  - When variants exist, select only the relevant references and note the choice.
- Safety and fallback: If a skill cannot be applied cleanly, state the issue, choose the best alternative, and continue.

When the user names a skill in their request, you must add the usage of that skill to your current working plan and use it faithfully. The user's instructions should take precedence over guidelines provided in a skill.

Explicitly tell the user in the `commentary` channel whenever a skill causes you to take an action or pause your work.

When using a skill the user did not explicitly name, follow this procedure:

- First, tell the user in the commentary channel **why** you are using the skill.
- Then, use the skill as long as it stays within the scope of the task.
- Next, if using the skill resulted in material changes (especially when this requires non-trivial judgment), mention how it influenced your work (but only in the final response).

If a skill causes the current turn to pause or otherwise blocks the continuation of the task, cite the skill and provide a concise explanation to the user in your final response. Do not cite skills you merely inspected.

99	call_CjLV1ujPOwVmClV1TIEolp0I	const groupDescription = `## Executive summary

Add workspace-level skill groups so Skillplane can organize related skills by domain and associate workspace members with those groups—for example Design, Marketing, Development, and Sales.

## Problem or opportunity

A flat workspace skill catalog does not express which skills belong together or which members should work with a domain-specific collection. As the catalog and workspace membership grow, discovery, onboarding, and administration become harder.

## Expected outcome

Workspace administrators can define reusable skill groups, associate skills and members with them, and inspect those relationships. Members can quickly find the skills relevant to their domains.

## Goals

- Create, rename, describe, archive, and restore skill groups within a workspace.
- Associate skills with skill groups.
- Associate workspace members with skill groups.

- Product teams that publish an official skill alongside their application code.
- Skill collection maintainers managing many skills in one repository.
- Workspace administrators connecting and monitoring external sources.
- Skill consumers who need trustworthy provenance and freshness.
- Security and operations teams responsible for repository credentials, supply-chain risk, sync reliability, and audits.

## Core user journeys

### Connect one official skill file

A Diffpanel maintainer connects a repository, chooses an allowed ref policy and \`skills/diffpanel-chapters/SKILL.md\`, previews the imported content, then creates or links the managed Skillplane skill. A maintainer registers a collection repository once. Skillplane discovers supported skill roots, previews additions/updates/conflicts, and creates explicit bindings from each managed skill to the common source.

### Inspect source provenance

A user opens a source page and sees all managed skills derived from it, their source paths, resolved commit SHAs, content digests, last sync results, drift, and failures.

### Recover from upstream changes

If a file is renamed, deleted, malformed, or conflicts with another binding, Skillplane reports a non-destructive action state rather than silently deleting or overwriting managed skills.

## Product principles

- Git is the authoring source; Skillplane remains the immutable distribution, authorization, review, audit, and context control plane.
- Every imported version must resolve to an immutable commit, even when tracking a mutable branch.
- Repository content is untrusted input and is never executed during import.
- Sync behavior must be previewable, idempotent, attributable, and recoverable.
- One shared source object should support both single-file and repository-scale modes.
- Existing manually managed skills do not change until explicitly connected.

### Ref strategy

- **Commit pin:** maximally reproducible, but updates require explicit ref changes.
- **Tracked branch/tag:** convenient continuous updates, but every sync must resolve and record a commit.
- **Proposal:** support both, with branch tracking producing immutable commit-backed sync runs.

### Sync trigger

- Manual sync is simplest and easiest to reason about.
- Scheduled polling avoids provider-specific webhook setup but costs API quota.
- Webhooks improve freshness but require installation lifecycle and replay protection.
- **Proposal:** manual first, then configurable webhook or schedule after reliability is proven.

- Import does not execute code or leak repository credentials.

- A preview should separate additions, updates, unchanged skills, removals, renames, and conflicts.

Backlog issue: [${sIssue}](${sUrl})

## Status

This is a proposed architecture based on the requested behavior and Skillplane's known immutable-version model. Exact repository services, database schema, provider abstractions, deployment topology, and UI code must be inspected before implementation.

## Current-state constraints

- Skillplane manages immutable skill bundles and published/candidate versions.
- Existing amendment policy controls review or trusted publication.
- Tenancy, visibility, authorization, audit, and contexts must remain authoritative.
- A mutable Git branch cannot replace immutable Skillplane version identity.
- Exact current Git integration capabilities are **not yet defined**.

## Proposed component model

### Git source registry

A workspace-scoped source record representing a repository and connection policy.

Proposed fields:

- source ID and workspace ID;
- canonical provider/repository identity and display URL;
- default ref strategy: pinned commit, tracked branch, or tracked tag;
- credential connection reference for private access, never a raw secret;
- discovery mode and optional manifest path;
- sync policy and current status;
- created/updated/archived timestamps and actor attribution.

### Skill source binding

Connects one managed skill to one path in a source.

Proposed fields:

- source ID and skill ID;
- repository-relative skill root or \`SKILL.md\` path;
- optional per-binding ref override;
- discovery key or upstream identity;
- last successful commit and content digest;
- drift/action state;
- unique constraints preventing ambiguous duplicate bindings.

### Sync run and per-binding result

Records one immutable synchronization attempt:

- requested ref and resolved commit SHA;
- trigger and actor;
- start/end timestamps;
- repository tree digest where useful;
- per-skill added/changed/unchanged/missing/conflict/error outcomes;
- candidate/version IDs created;
- sanitized provider diagnostics.

### Version provenance

Every source-created candidate/version should retain:

- source ID;
- repository identity and URL;
- resolved commit SHA;
- source path;
- source content/bundle digest;
- sync run ID;
- import actor and policy outcome.

## Synchronization pipeline

1. Authorize the actor for the workspace and source.
2. Resolve repository connection and credential reference.
3. Resolve the requested branch/tag/commit to an exact commit SHA.
4. Fetch a bounded tree or required paths through a constrained provider adapter.
5. Discover skill roots deterministically.
6. Validate paths, file types, sizes, manifests, bundle limits, and metadata.
7. Build the canonical Skillplane file set without executing repository code.
8. Compare source digests with current bindings and managed versions.
9. Produce a preview: add, update, unchanged, missing, renamed candidate, or conflict.
10. On confirmed apply, create/import through existing immutable version and amendment-policy services.
11. Persist sync results and provenance transactionally where possible.
12. Read back created candidates/versions and update source health.

A no-op comparison must not create a new version.

## Single-file mode

- User supplies source, ref policy, and one \`SKILL.md\` or skill-root path.
- Validation confirms the path belongs to the resolved repository tree.
- The binding maps exactly one managed skill to that path.
- The Diffpanel example uses repository-relative path \`skills/diffpanel-chapters/SKILL.md\`; the canonical repository URL remains to be supplied.

## Repository-wide mode

**Proposal:** support a deterministic discovery precedence:

1. explicit repository manifest, if defined;
2. recognized skill metadata files;
3. bounded recursive discovery of \`SKILL.md\` roots.

The final convention is **not yet defined**. Discovery must preview every candidate and flag duplicate slugs, nested roots, unsupported bundles, and conflicting existing bindings.

One source detail endpoint/view returns all bindings with path, managed skill, resolved commit, digest, sync result, and drift state.

## Provider abstraction

Define a narrow interface for:

- canonicalize repository identity;
- verify access;
- resolve ref to commit;
- list bounded tree;
- fetch bounded blobs;
- register/verify webhooks if supported;
- expose rate-limit and retry metadata.

Initial provider selection is open. Public GitHub is a likely first candidate because the supplied collection example is GitHub-hosted, but this is a proposal, not a confirmed requirement.

## Security and supply-chain controls

- Never execute hooks, package scripts, binaries, or repository code.
- Reject absolute paths, traversal, symlink escape, unsafe submodules, unsupported media, and decompression bombs.
- Bound file count, per-file bytes, expanded bundle bytes, repository traversal depth, and total sync work.
- Treat manifests and Markdown as untrusted data.
- Store private-repository authorization as scoped credential references with rotation and revocation.
- Redact tokens and provider headers from logs and audit.
- Verify webhook signatures, timestamps, replay IDs, installation identity, and repository binding.
- Require workspace and skill authorization at both preview and apply.
- Preserve existing visibility rules; a public repository does not automatically make a managed skill public.
- Surface commit verification/signature information as evidence if available, without treating it as sufficient trust on its own.

## Concurrency and idempotency

- Key sync application by source, resolved commit, discovery configuration, and content digest.
- Use per-source serialization or optimistic concurrency to avoid racing webhook/manual runs.
- Make apply replay-safe after timeouts.
- Do not recreate successful candidates or bindings when recovering partial runs.
- For repository-wide sync, persist per-binding results so failed items can be retried without duplicating successful items.

## Rename and deletion handling

- Missing upstream paths mark bindings as action required; they do not archive or delete managed skills automatically.
- Rename detection may use explicit upstream IDs, manifest keys, or digest similarity, but requires confirmation when ambiguous.
- Source removal disconnects future synchronization while preserving immutable versions and provenance.
- Force-push or unreachable historical commits must be visible; previously recorded provenance remains immutable.

## API/MCP surface

**Proposal:** paginated, authorization-filtered operations for:

- create/get/list/update/archive/restore sources;
- validate connection and preview discovery;
- list source bindings and grouped skills;
- create/update/remove a binding;
- start/get/list sync runs;
- preview and apply repository-wide changes;
- filter skills by source and source status.

Exact tool/route names and least-privilege scopes are **not yet defined**. Long-running sync should use asynchronous jobs with status polling or events rather than holding a request open.

## Reliability and observability

Track:

- source access and auth failures;
- ref resolution latency and errors;
- provider rate limit and retry state;
- discovered/changed/unchanged/conflicting counts;
- no-op ratio;
- candidate/publication outcomes;
- webhook signature/replay failures;
- sync duration, queue age, partial failures, and recovery;
- drift age per binding.

Alerting should distinguish provider outage, expired credentials, malformed repository content, policy rejection, and internal persistence failure.

## Migration and compatibility

- Add source records and optional bindings without changing existing skills.
- Existing manual publish/amend flows remain authoritative and available.
- A manually managed skill is connected only through an explicit, confirmed operation.
- Define behavior for manual amendments to a source-bound skill before launch: reject, allow as divergence, or support overlays.
- Rollback disables synchronization and webhooks while preserving source records, bindings, runs, versions, and provenance.

## Delivery sequence

### Phase 1: source and provenance contracts

- Decide providers, ref policies, discovery convention, credential model, and manual-edit behavior.
- Define schema, provider interface, provenance, API/MCP contracts, and limits.
- Threat-model public and private source ingestion.

### Phase 2: public single-file source

- Implement public repository access, commit resolution, constrained file fetch, validation, preview, binding, and manual sync.
- Integrate changed content with existing amendment policy.
- Deliver source provenance on skill/version views.

### Phase 3: repository-wide discovery

- Add deterministic discovery and preview.
- Add bulk binding/apply with per-item idempotency and recovery.
- Deliver source detail and filter/group views.

### Phase 4: private sources and automation

- Add scoped credential connections and rotation.
- Add webhook and/or scheduled synchronization after deciding trigger policy.
- Add signature validation, replay protection, rate-limit handling, queues, and retries.

### Phase 5: hardening and ecosystem integration

- Load/performance tests for large repositories.
- Rename/transfer/fork handling.
- skills.sh integration only after its role and contract are defined.
- Operational dashboards, alerts, and recovery tooling.

## Validation

- Unit tests for URL canonicalization, ref resolution, path validation, discovery, digesting, and provenance.
- Contract tests against supported provider APIs.
- Security tests for traversal, symlinks, submodules, oversized files, malicious manifests, secret redaction, and webhook replay.
- Idempotency and concurrency tests for repeated/racing syncs.
- Integration tests from repository commit to candidate/version and policy outcome.
- Repository-wide partial-failure and recovery tests.
- Cross-workspace and private-source authorization denial tests.
- UI tests for source setup, preview, apply, source grouping, drift, and failure recovery.
- Production canary with a controlled public repository before broader rollout.

## Risks and mitigations

- **Supply-chain compromise:** immutable commit provenance, review policy, no execution, and visible diffs.
- **Credential leakage:** provider connections, least scopes, redaction, rotation, and audit.
- **Mutable refs/force-pushes:** resolve every run to a commit and preserve prior provenance.
- **Provider outages/rate limits:** queueing, backoff, status distinction, and manual retry.
- **Mass unintended changes:** preview, bounded batches, policy gates, and non-destructive deletion handling.
- **Layout ambiguity:** explicit manifest precedence and conflict states.
- **State divergence:** define manual-edit/overlay behavior before source binding launch.

## Open questions

Provider scope, ref semantics, trigger modes, repository layout, overlay behavior, rename/deletion policy, source transfer identity, and skills.sh integration are blocking design decisions for later phases.`;

## Goals

- Represent a Git source with repository identity, provider, ref policy, credentials where needed, and provenance.
- Configure an individual managed skill from one Git-hosted \`SKILL.md\` path.

- Show and filter all skills associated with the same source.

- Can one managed skill combine Git-sourced files with Skillplane-managed overlays?
- How are forks and repository transfers represented without losing provenance?

## Context and motivating problem

Skillplane currently presents a workspace's skills without a domain grouping layer. A flat catalog becomes harder to navigate and administer as the number of skills and members grows. The requested capability is to group skills into areas such as Design, Marketing, Development, and Sales, then associate workspace members with the relevant groups.

This document captures product intent. It does not authorize implementation, staffing, or dates.

## Target users and stakeholders

- Workspace owners and administrators who organize skills and membership.
- Workspace members who need a focused view of domain-relevant skills.
- Skill authors and maintainers who need discoverability without duplicating skills.
- Security and operations stakeholders responsible for authorization and auditability.
- Agent clients that may eventually consume group-aware skill discovery through APIs or MCP.

## Core use cases

### Organize a domain catalog

An administrator creates a “Design” group, adds design-related skills, and sees the group as one coherent collection.

### Onboard a workspace member

An administrator associates a new designer with the Design group. The member can discover the skills relevant to that domain without searching the full catalog.

### Support cross-functional work

A member or skill may need to appear in more than one domain, such as Design and Marketing.

**Proposal:** model both relationships as many-to-many. This is not yet a confirmed decision.

### Audit and maintain groups

An administrator can inspect membership, understand who changed it, archive an obsolete group, and preserve historical evidence without deleting the underlying skills or members.

## Product principles

- Groups are workspace-scoped and cannot reference another workspace's records.
- Groups complement workspace roles; they do not replace owner, admin, editor, or viewer semantics.
- Membership is explicit. Skillplane should not infer it from titles, activity, or private data.
- Archive is preferred over destructive deletion when relationships or audit history exist.
- Existing workspaces remain valid with zero groups.

## Ideas discussed and product options

### Option A: organizational grouping only

Groups drive labels, navigation, filtering, and onboarding but do not change authorization.

- Lower security risk and simpler initial delivery.
- Does not solve cases where group membership is intended to grant access.

### Option B: group-based skill availability

A member's groups determine which workspace skills are available to them.

- Stronger delegation and least-privilege potential.
- Creates a new authorization layer and requires careful precedence rules.

### Option C: separate organization and access controls

A group organizes skills and members, while an explicit policy flag or separate access policy determines whether it grants availability.

- More expressive and safer long term.
- Higher conceptual and implementation complexity.

**Open question:** which option reflects the intended first release? The request supports organization and member association, but does not establish access-control semantics.

## Desired outcomes and success measures

- Administrators can create domain groups and maintain skill/member associations without duplicates.
- Members find relevant skills with fewer catalog searches.
- Group filters and detail views return consistent results across UI and API surfaces.
- No group operation leaks or links cross-workspace records.
- Group archival and membership changes remain auditable.
- Existing workspaces and skills require no migration action to continue working.
- If groups affect authorization, permission tests show no accidental access widening.

Potential quantitative measures are not yet defined. Candidate measures include time to onboard a member, skill discovery success, percentage of skills organized, and failed/unauthorized group mutations.

## Product and UX considerations

- Group names should be clear within a workspace; uniqueness rules need definition.
- Group cards or rows should show skill and member counts.
- Skill and member detail views should expose group membership.
- Filtering should support one or multiple groups if many-to-many is adopted.
- Empty groups should be valid during setup.
- Archived groups should disappear from normal selection while remaining recoverable.
- Bulk assignment may be important for large workspaces but should not obscure per-item failures.
- UI language must distinguish “workspace role,” “skill group,” and “access policy.”

## Operational considerations

- Every create, rename, archive, restore, and association change should be attributable.
- Bulk changes need bounded request sizes, idempotency, and clear partial-failure handling.
- Group membership counts and filters need pagination at scale.
- Support tooling should make effective membership and, if applicable, effective access explainable.

## Goals

- Workspace-level skill groups.
- Skill-to-group and member-to-group associations.
- Bidirectional inspection and filtering.
- Safe lifecycle and audit behavior.
- Explicit authorization semantics before production rollout.

## Non-goals

- Replacing workspace roles.
- Automatic group inference.
- Cross-workspace or organization-global groups in the initial scope.
- Nested group hierarchies unless separately approved.
- Automatic modification of skill content.

## Acceptance criteria

- Domain groups such as Design, Marketing, Development, and Sales can be represented.
- Authorized administrators can add and remove skills and members idempotently.
- Group, skill, and member views expose consistent associations.
- Search/list operations can filter by group.
- Cross-workspace associations fail safely.
- Archiving a group does not delete skills, members, or audit history.
- Existing ungrouped workspaces continue to work.
- Documentation and UI clearly state whether membership is organizational or access-bearing.

## Assumptions

- A workspace is the tenancy boundary.
- Existing skill and member identifiers remain canonical.
- Existing workspace roles continue to govern who may administer workspace configuration.

## Open questions

- Does group membership grant access, set defaults, or only categorize?
- Can members and skills belong to multiple groups?
- Can admins manage groups, or only owners?
- Are groups available in personal workspaces?
- Are nested groups needed later?
- How should removing a member from a group affect active agent sessions or cached discovery?
- Is bulk assignment required for the first release?`;
